books.section: Topic 4.11 An Age of Reform, A. Reform Movements in the Antebellum Period

primary_sources: Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843

stimulus.text: "I come to present the strong claims of suffering humanity. . . . I proceed, Gentlemen, briefly to call your attention to the present state of Insane Persons confined within this Commonwealth, in cages, closets, cellars, stalls, pens! Chained, naked, beaten with rods, and lashed into obedience!" — Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts, 1843
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from Dorothea Dix, Memorial to the Legislature of Massachusetts (Boston: Munroe & Francis, 1843). Wording checked against the full text at the Disability History Museum and the American Journal of Public Health reprint; ellipses mark omissions.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from Dix, Memorial (1843)
stem: Dix's memorial best illustrates which feature of antebellum reform?

options.text: Reformers seeking a federal constitutional amendment from Congress
options.misconception: Dix petitioned a state legislature, not Congress, and asked for no amendment.

options.text: Reform led by the Democratic Party and its leaders
options.misconception: Democrats were skeptical of expanded government; reform drew more Whig support.

options.text: Women using investigation and petitions to move state governments

options.misconception: Dix asks the government to build asylums; she wants more state action, not less.

rationales.A: Dix's memorial went to the Massachusetts legislature and asked it to expand the Worcester asylum. No constitutional amendment was involved.
rationales.B: Democrats tended to oppose the expanded government reformers called for. Reform energy ran more through Whigs and voluntary societies.
rationales.C: Dix, a woman with no office, investigated jails herself and petitioned the legislature. Her memorial moved Massachusetts to expand its asylum.
rationales.D: Dix's whole plea asks the state to act and spend. Rejecting government action is the opposite of her memorial.
rationales.general:
1. Note who speaks. Dix is a woman with no office, addressing the legislature as a petitioner.
2. Note how she speaks. She brings facts from her own visits to jails and almshouses.
3. Note the result. Her petition moved the state to expand the Worcester asylum.
Background: Women, barred from voting and office, used moral reform societies and petitions to enter public life.
Remember: when a reformer has no vote, watch for the petition — it is her way into government.
